summary: TLS 1.3 fixes known weaknesses of TLS 1.2 and its use is growing. This document says that no further changes will be approved for TLS 1.2, except urgent security fixes, new TLS exporter labels, and new ALPN protocol IDs.

eli5.summary: An old tool still works, but the toolmakers say they will stop adding new features to it. Only emergency repairs are allowed, and everyone should move to the newer one.

questions: what is the tls 1.2 feature freeze
subtitle: No more changes to TLS 1.2 beyond urgent security fixes, so new work, including post-quantum, goes to TLS 1.3.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 fixes most known deficiencies of TLS 1.2 and its use is growing, yet both versions have extension points that allow new features to keep being added to the older one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says no changes will be approved for TLS 1.2 outside urgent security fixes, new TLS exporter labels and new ALPN protocol IDs. A note in the other TLS registries marks new entries as intended for TLS 1.3 or later.
tldr.outcome: Post-quantum cryptography will not be specified for TLS 1.2, so anyone wishing to deploy it should expect to use TLS 1.3. The freeze does not apply to DTLS.

facts.label: Allowed TLS 1.2 changes
facts.value: Urgent security fixes, exporter labels, ALPN IDs

today: RFC 9851 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Freeze
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 fixes most known deficiencies of TLS 1.2. The RFC gives as examples that it encrypts more of the traffic so outsiders cannot read it, and removes most cryptographic primitives now considered weak. It also enjoys robust security proofs.

Both versions have extension points, so items such as new cryptographic algorithms and new supported groups can be added without defining a new protocol. This document specifies that no changes will be approved for TLS 1.2 outside urgent security fixes (as decided by TLS Working Group consensus) and the registry exceptions below. It applies to TLS only, not to DTLS in any version.
sections.eli5: The old version still works, but the builders will only fix emergencies on it. All the new features go into the newer version.

sections.title: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography Matters Here
sections.content:
The RFC explains that cryptographically relevant quantum computers, once available, are likely to greatly lessen the time and effort needed to break RSA, finite-field Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curve cryptography, which TLS uses today. NIST began a multi-year effort in 2016 to standardize algorithms that will be safe afterwards, and in 2024 released standards for ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.

Several IETF working groups, including TLS, are working on hybrid algorithms and identifiers for the transition. The TLS Working Group's effort is focused exclusively on TLS 1.3 or later. In the RFC's blunt words, post-quantum cryptography for TLS 1.2 will not be specified at any time.
sections.eli5: One day, super-powerful computers might crack today's secret codes. The new codes are being built only for the newer version, so you need to move to it to get them.

sections.title: What Still Changes: Registry Rules
sections.content:
No TLS registries are closed. Instead the instructions to IANA and the TLS Designated Experts are modified to limit what can be added. There are no new limits on two registries: TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs and TLS Exporter Labels.

The other TLS registries get a note saying that any entry added after the IESG approves publication of RFC 9851 is intended for TLS 1.3 or later and makes no similar requirement on DTLS. Such entries should carry an informal indication like "For TLS 1.3 or later", for example in the Comment column. The note was added to registries including TLS Cipher Suites, TLS ExtensionType Values, TLS Supported Groups and TLS SignatureScheme.
sections.eli5: The big list of allowed things gets a sticker: anything new is for the newer version only. Two small lists stay open as before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The whole document is about security. The RFC offers post-quantum security concerns as an additional reason to upgrade to TLS 1.3.
sections.eli5: The reason for the whole rule is staying safe, and moving to the newer version is the safe choice.
